# Part 1 - Reproducible Report and Data Description
## 1.1 Introduction

For this homework, I have selected the Student Performance dataset. 
This dataset uses a response variable of Final Score, with three predictors: the amount of study hours per week,
the students attendance as a percentage, and the students prior score. The goal of this homework is to fit and
diagnose a linear model using matrix computation.

## 1.2 Data Inspection and Validation

```{python}
import pandas as pd

print(data.head())
```

The first five raws of data are `{python} data.head()`

columns. The IDs are also unique.

# Part 2 - Matrix Setup and Standardization

Convert the predictors and response to NumPy arrays
```{python}
import numpy as np

predictors = data[
    ["study_hours_per_week", "attendance_pct", "prior_score"]
].to_numpy()

y = data["final_score"].to_numpy()
```

Standardize the predictors
```{python}
means = predictors.mean(axis=0)
sds = predictors.std(axis=0)

Z = (
    predictors - means
) / sds

Z.mean(axis=0), Z.std(axis=0)
```

Construct the design matrix
```{python}
X = np.column_stack([
    np.ones(len(Z)),
    Z
])
```

The shape of predictors is `{python} predictors.shape`

The shape of Z is `{python} Z.shape`

The shape of X is `{python} X.shape`

The shape of y is `{python} y.shape`

The rank of X is `{python} int(np.linalg.matrix_rank(X))`

The number of predictors is 1 less than the rank of X: `{python} int(np.linalg.matrix_rank(X) - 1)`

X and y must have compatible shapes because otherwise matrix operations (such as addition or multiplication) between
them wouldn't work. We include the intercept column in the X matrix because that will tell us what the
$\widehat{\beta_0}$ that we calculate will be. Standardizing the predictors was done so that we can more easily
compare the distribution to a normal distribution, with the standardized predictors now reporting how many standard
deviations away from the mean they are. Broadcasting made this standardization possible with out a Python loop because
in the Z calculation, it was implied that each element in the predictors array was to be subtracted by the mean of that
row, so a loop was not needed to iterate through each element in the predictors array individually. The same is true
for dividing by the sds of each row. It was implied that each element in the (predictors - mean) array was to be
divided by the sds, so a loop iterating through each element is not needed.

# Part 3 - Least Squares

Fit the model:
```{python}
beta_hat, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)

beta_hat
```

The intercept of this model is approximately `{python} round(float(beta_hat[0]), 4)` points of final score

The coefficient of the standardized study hours per week predictor is approximately
`{python} round(float(beta_hat[1]), 4)`

The coefficient of the standardized attendance percentage predictor is approximately
`{python} round(float(beta_hat[2]), 4)`

The coefficient of the standarized prior score predictor is approximately
`{python} round(float(beta_hat[3]), 4)`

Out of the three standardized predictors, prior score has the largest absolute value coefficient

Calculate fitted values:
```{python}
fitted = X @ beta_hat
```

Calculate residuals:
```{python}
residuals = y - fitted
```

The mean of the residuals is approximately `{python} round(float(residuals.mean()), 5)`

And the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) is approximately:
```{python}
rmse = np.sqrt(
    np.mean(
        residuals ** 2
    )
)

round(float(rmse), 4)
```

X @ beta_hat represents our approximation of the response values given the predictor values. So X @ beta_hat
gives us the y_hat values, which are the y-values of our linear regression model. The residual mean should be near
zero when an intercept is present because the residuals measure how far off from our prediction model the actual
measured values are, and for a normal distribution the residuals should have equal variance and have a mean of
0. The Root Mean Square Errors (RMSE) summarizes the square root of the average squared distance between the actual
measured values and the predicted values, and this is helpful as it returns an error in the original units of the
response variable. The difference between X @ beta_hat and X * beta_hat is that the @ operator is matrix
multiplication, whereas the * operator signifies element wise mutliplication. So the * operator multiplies
each element of X with the same element of beta_hat, but that is not the matrix multiplication that we want for this
operation. We want mathematical matrix multiplication, which uses the @ symbol.
